title: Section 49 Registration Act — Effect of non-registration

content.overview: Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 is the effect of non-registration. A document required to be registered by section 17, or by any provision of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, shall not, unless registered, affect any immovable property comprised in it, or confer any power to adopt, or be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property or conferring such power. The proviso allows an unregistered document affecting immovable property, and required to be registered, to be received as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance, or as evidence of any collateral transaction not required to be effected by a registered instrument, and for the purpose of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 49 does not apply to a document that registration law does not require to be registered.
content.study: Ask first whether registration was compulsory. If it was, apply the three bars: no effect on the immovable property, no power to adopt, and no evidence of that transaction. Then test the proviso. Do not treat the proviso as permission to prove title.

learningObjectives: Limit the proviso to contract, collateral transaction and section 53A.
Apply section 49 only to a document that was required to be registered.
enhancement.definition: Section 49 bars an unregistered compulsorily registrable document from affecting immovable property, conferring a power to adopt, or being evidence of that transaction, subject to the proviso.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Non-registration does not erase every fact. It blocks the document from operating as the transaction that the law required to be registered, with a narrow evidentiary proviso.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Registration Act, 1908, section 49, read with section 17. Transfer of Property Act section 53A is named in the proviso and is not reopened as a TPA topic.
essentialIngredients: Document required to be registered under section 17 or the Transfer of Property Act
Bar on affecting immovable property comprised in it
Bar on conferring a power to adopt
Bar on receiving it as evidence of that transaction
Proviso: specific performance, collateral transaction, or section 53A
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The section is the sanction for the compulsory list. The first bar is substantive: the document does not affect the immovable property. The second is the adoption-power bar. The third is evidentiary: it is not received as evidence of the transaction affecting that property or conferring that power. The proviso is an exception to reception as evidence, not a revival of the conveyance. It permits use as evidence of a contract in a specific-performance suit, as evidence of a collateral transaction that did not itself have to be effected by a registered instrument, and for section 53A part performance. A party who tenders the unregistered sale deed as proof of title is outside the proviso. A party who tenders it only to show the contract sued on in specific performance is inside the first proviso limb. What counts as collateral is case-law and is not defined by a new holding here.
examples: An unregistered sale deed of land is tendered to prove title. Section 49 bars that use.
The same deed is tendered in a specific-performance suit as evidence of the contract. The proviso permits that reception.
An unregistered will is tendered. Section 17 did not require its registration, so section 49 does not apply.
enhancement.problemApplication: Confirm compulsory registration. If yes, apply the three bars. Allow the document only for a proviso purpose. Do not let a collateral label smuggle in the title itself.
distinctions: Effect on property vs evidence of a contract
Section 49 bar vs section 18 optional document
Collateral transaction vs the transaction required to be registered
Section 49 vs a fresh suit for title
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Collateral-purpose and part-performance readings remain on the case-law gate.
enhancement.shortAnswerStructure: An unregistered document that had to be registered does not affect the immovable property or prove that transaction, except for specific performance, a collateral transaction, or section 53A.

keyTakeaways: Section 49 applies only if registration was required.
The document does not affect the immovable property.
It is not evidence of that transaction.
The proviso covers specific performance, a collateral transaction, and section 53A.
The proviso does not prove title.
authoritativeSources: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, section 53A, as named in the proviso

verification.note: Section 49 and its proviso stated from the Act. Collateral-transaction case law not invented. TPA subject not reopened.
